# Introduction

The sinking of the RMS *Titanic* on April 15, 1912 remains one of the best-documented maritime disasters in modern history. Historical and sociological studies have shown that survival was strongly shaped by evacuation norms ("women and children first") and differences in social class [@hall1986; @elinder2012].

In this project, we ask a predictive research question: **how accurately can a passenger's survival on the Titanic be predicted from demographic and ticket information available prior to departure, and does adding domain-informed optional features and interactions improve upon our core correlation-selected predictors?** Using the Kaggle Titanic dataset [@cukierski2012], we first conduct an exploratory data analysis on the development set and save the cleaned datasets to the processed data folder. We then build and evaluate a regularized logistic regression classification model using five-fold stratified cross-validation and an independent held-out test set.

# Exploratory data analysis

This section explores the Titanic passenger data before any model is built. We check the structure of the data and how much of it is missing, compare every passenger characteristic with the outcome we want to predict (whether the passenger survived, coded 1, or died, coded 0), and clean and transform the data so that it is ready for modelling. We finish by ranking the features by how strongly they relate to survival and choosing the four to five that we will carry into the model.

We use Python with pandas [@mckinney2010], scikit-learn [@pedregosa2011], matplotlib [@hunter2007] and seaborn [@waskom2021]. The passenger records come from the Kaggle "Titanic: Machine Learning from Disaster" competition [@cukierski2012]. Each row is one passenger. Kaggle supplies two files: a training file of 891 passengers whose survival outcome is known, and a test file of 418 passengers whose outcome is hidden.

```{python}
#| label: setup
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Patch
import seaborn as sns
from IPython.display import display
from sklearn.feature_selection import mutual_info_classif
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
import shutil
import subprocess
from zipfile import ZipFile

SEED = 522  # fixed seed so that every teammate gets the same mutual-information values
sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid", context="notebook")
plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "axes.titlesize": 12, "axes.labelsize": 11})
SURV, DIED = "#0072B2", "#D55E00"
PALETTE = {"Survived": SURV, "Did not survive": DIED}

# The report is rendered from analysis/, so the data folder is one level up.
def find_root(start=Path.cwd()):
    for p in [start, *start.parents]:
        if (p / "pyproject.toml").exists():
            return p
    return start
ROOT = find_root()
RAW_DIR, PROC_DIR = ROOT / "data" / "raw", ROOT / "data" / "processed"

RAW_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
PROC_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

# Download the Kaggle data if the raw CSV files are not already present.
train_path = RAW_DIR / "train.csv"
test_path = RAW_DIR / "test.csv"

if not (train_path.exists() and test_path.exists()):
    kaggle_executable = shutil.which("kaggle")

    if kaggle_executable is None:
        raise RuntimeError(
            "Kaggle CLI was not found. Run `uv sync` to install project dependencies."
        )

    print("Downloading Titanic data from Kaggle...")

    subprocess.run(
        [
            kaggle_executable,
            "competitions",
            "download",
            "-c",
            "titanic",
            "-p",
            str(RAW_DIR),
        ],
        check=True,
    )

    zip_path = RAW_DIR / "titanic.zip"

    # Extract the downloaded CSV files into data/raw/.
    with ZipFile(zip_path, "r") as zip_file:
        zip_file.extractall(RAW_DIR)

    # Check that both required files were extracted.
    missing_files = [
        filename
        for filename in ["train.csv", "test.csv"]
        if not (RAW_DIR / filename).exists()
    ]

    if missing_files:
        raise FileNotFoundError(
            f"Expected files were not found after extraction: {missing_files}"
        )

    # Remove the ZIP file after extraction.
    zip_path.unlink()

    print("Titanic data downloaded and extracted successfully.")

else:
    print("Raw Titanic data already exists. Skipping download.")

# Read the raw data.
train = pd.read_csv(train_path)
test = pd.read_csv(test_path)

train, holdout = train_test_split(
    train,
    test_size=0.30,
    stratify=train["Survived"],
    random_state=SEED
)

print(f"Training data: {train.shape[0]} rows x {train.shape[1]} columns")
print(f"Test data: {test.shape[0]} rows x {test.shape[1]} columns")
```

## Training and test data

The Kaggle Titanic dataset consists of two files: `train.csv`, containing 891 passengers with known survival outcomes, and `test.csv`, containing 418 passengers whose survival outcomes are withheld. To enable independent model evaluation, we partition the 891 labeled observations into a training set (70%) and a held-out test set (30%) using stratified random sampling to preserve approximately the original proportions of survivors and non-survivors.

We use the new training set for exploratory data analysis, preprocessing decisions, and model development. The held-out test set is reserved for final performance evaluation, while Kaggle's original `test.csv` remains separate for generating predictions.

## The variables

Table 1 describes each column in the data. The last column of the table says what we expect to do with it, which we justify in the sections below.

| Column in the data | Meaning | Plan |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Survived | Outcome: 1 if the passenger survived, 0 if not (the target) | Target |
| Pclass | Ticket class: 1 (first), 2 (second) or 3 (third) | Candidate |
| Sex | Male or female | Candidate |
| Age | Age in years (fractional for infants) | Candidate, needs imputation |
| SibSp | Number of siblings or spouses travelling with the passenger | Used to build family size |
| Parch | Number of parents or children travelling with the passenger | Used to build family size |
| Fare | Ticket price in pounds | Candidate, log transform |
| Cabin | Cabin number, mostly missing | Reduced to a cabin-recorded flag |
| Embarked | Port of boarding: Cherbourg, Queenstown or Southampton | Candidate, needs imputation |
| Name | Passenger name including title (for example Mr or Mrs) | Only the title is used |
| Ticket | Ticket number | Excluded |
| PassengerId | Row identifier | Excluded (identifier only) |

*Table 1. Description of each column in the Titanic data and how we plan to use it.*

## Missing data

We now measure how much of each column is missing in the training set. For comparison we also count the missing values in the test file, because it will be cleaned in the same way later. These counts do not influence any decision.

```{python}
#| label: missing-table

missing = pd.DataFrame({
    "Training: missing (n)": train[cols].isna().sum(),
    "Training: missing (%)": (train[cols].isna().mean() * 100).round(1),
    "Test: missing (n)": test[cols].isna().sum(),
    "Test: missing (%)": (test[cols].isna().mean() * 100).round(1),
})
missing = missing[(missing.iloc[:, [0, 2]] > 0).any(axis=1)].sort_values(
    "Training: missing (%)", ascending=False
)
missing
```

*Table 3. Columns with missing values in the training data and in the test data.*

*Figure 2. Percentage of missing values per column. The two files have very similar gaps, so one cleaning recipe can serve both.*

Cabin is missing for 77.4% of training passengers (482 of 623), age for 19.7% (123), and port of boarding for only 0.2% (1). The test file shows the same pattern for cabin (78.2%) and age (20.6%), and has one missing fare. No other column has gaps.

Missing values are not always random, so we check whether being missing is itself related to survival.

```{python}
#| label: helpers
overall = train["Survived"].mean()

def rate_bar(ax, data, col, order=None, xlabel="", labels=None):
    """Bar chart of the survival rate for each level of `col`, with group sizes."""
    g = data.groupby(col, observed=True)["Survived"].agg(["mean", "size"])
    if order is not None:
        g = g.reindex(order)
    names = labels if labels is not None else [str(i) for i in g.index]
    bars = ax.bar(names, g["mean"] * 100, color=SURV)
    for b, m, n in zip(bars, g["mean"], g["size"]):
        ax.text(b.get_x() + b.get_width() / 2, m * 100 + 1.5, f"{m:.0%}\n(n={n})",
                ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=9)
    ax.axhline(overall * 100, ls="--", color="grey", lw=1, label="Overall survival rate (38%)")
    ax.set_ylim(0, 115)
    ax.set_yticks(range(0, 101, 20))
    ax.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=8, frameon=False)
    ax.set_xlabel(xlabel)
    ax.set_ylabel("Survival rate (%)")

flags = train.assign(AgeKnown=train["Age"].notna(), CabinKnown=train["Cabin"].notna())
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

#### Age recorded? {.unnumbered}

```{python}
#| label: plot-missing-age
#| fig-alt: "Bar chart: passengers with a missing age survived 28% of the time versus 41% with a recorded age."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
rate_bar(ax, flags, "AgeKnown", order=[False, True], xlabel="Age recorded?", labels=["No", "Yes"])
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

#### Cabin recorded? {.unnumbered}

```{python}
#| label: plot-missing-cabin
#| fig-alt: "Bar chart: passengers with no cabin recorded survived 29% of the time versus 70% with a cabin recorded."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
rate_bar(ax, flags, "CabinKnown", order=[False, True], xlabel="Cabin recorded?", labels=["No", "Yes"])
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

:::

*Figure 3. Survival rate by whether age and cabin were recorded. Use the tabs to switch between the two. The dashed line is the overall survival rate, and numbers in brackets are group sizes.*

Passengers with no recorded age survived approximately 28% of the time compared with 41% for those with a recorded age, and passengers with no recorded cabin survived approximately 29% compared with 70% for those with a cabin. These differences suggest that missingness may be associated with survival, so it is worth keeping simple "was it recorded?" flags next to the imputed values. Cabin in particular tells us more through whether it exists than through its content, so we do not try to fill it in.

**Decisions for missing data.** We fill in age using the median age of passengers with the same title, because titles such as "Master" (boys) and "Mrs" separate age groups far better than one overall median. We fill the missing ports with the most common port, and the single missing fare in the test file with the median fare of the same ticket class. For cabin we keep only a yes/no flag. All fill-in values are learned from the training data only and then applied unchanged to the test data, so no information leaks from the test file. For predictive modelling, missing values are imputed separately within each cross-validation training fold using the median, preventing validation-fold information from influencing the fitted imputation values.

## Comparing each feature with survival

We now look at each feature on its own against survival. Throughout, the dashed line in the bar charts marks the overall survival rate of 38%.

```{python}
#| label: engineer-for-eda
def extract_title(names):
    """Pull the title (Mr, Mrs, ...) out of a passenger name and group the rare ones."""
    t = names.str.extract(r" ([A-Za-z]+)\.", expand=False)
    t = t.replace({"Mlle": "Miss", "Ms": "Miss", "Mme": "Mrs"})
    return t.where(t.isin(["Mr", "Mrs", "Miss", "Master"]), "Rare")

def add_simple_features(df):
    """Features that need no learned values, so they are safe to build on any dataset."""
    out = df.copy()
    out["Title"] = extract_title(out["Name"])
    out["FamilySize"] = out["SibSp"] + out["Parch"] + 1
    out["IsAlone"] = (out["FamilySize"] == 1).astype(int)
    out["HasCabin"] = out["Cabin"].notna().astype(int)
    out["AgeMissing"] = out["Age"].isna().astype(int)
    return out

eda = add_simple_features(eda)
```

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
```

#### Sex and class together {.unnumbered}

```{python}
#| label: plot-sex-class
#| fig-alt: "Grouped bar chart: women in first and second class survived above 90%, women in third class 50%, while men survived 37%, 16% and 14% in first, second and third class."
sc = eda.groupby(["Pclass", "Sex"])["Survived"].mean().unstack() * 100
sc.index = ["First", "Second", "Third"]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
sc[["female", "male"]].plot.bar(ax=ax, color=[SURV, DIED], rot=0, width=0.75)
ax.set_ylim(0, 112)
ax.set_xlabel("Passenger class")
ax.set_ylabel("Survival rate (%)")
ax.legend(["Female", "Male"], title="Sex", loc="upper right")
for c in ax.containers:
    ax.bar_label(c, fmt="%.0f%%", padding=2, fontsize=9)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

:::

*Figure 4. Survival rate by sex, by passenger class and by both together. Use the tabs to switch between the three views.*

Sex is the strongest single signal in the data. In the training data 74.2% of women survived compared with 18.9% of men (Figure 4, Sex tab). Survival also falls steadily with passenger class, from 63.0% in first class to 47.3% in second and 24.2% in third (Figure 4, Passenger class tab). Both patterns match historical accounts of the sinking, where women were prioritised for lifeboats and survival declined with social class [@hall1986; @elinder2012].

The third tab, "Sex and class together", shows that the two effects combine. Almost all women in first class (96.8%) and second class (92.1%) survived, but only half of the women in third class (50.0%). Men in every class did poorly, from 36.9% in first class down to 13.5% in third. This is an interaction: the effect of class depends on sex. A model that can capture interactions, or that includes both features, should do much better than one that uses either alone.

**Include in the model?** Yes, both sex and passenger class.

### Age

```{python}
#| label: prep-age
known_age = eda.dropna(subset=["Age"]).copy()
known_age["AgeGroup"] = pd.cut(
    known_age["Age"], [0, 12, 18, 35, 60, 100],
    labels=["0-12", "13-18", "19-35", "36-60", "61+"],
)
```

#### Age distribution {.unnumbered}

```{python}
#| fig-alt: "Overlapping density curves of age for survivors and non-survivors, with an extra peak of survivors under 10."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 4))
sns.kdeplot(data=known_age, x="Age", hue="Outcome", palette=PALETTE, fill=True,
            common_norm=False, alpha=0.4, ax=ax, clip=(0, 85))
ax.set_xlabel("Age (years)")
ax.set_ylabel("Density")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

#### Survival by age group {.unnumbered}

```{python}
#| label: plot-age-group
#| fig-alt: "Bar chart: survival is 61% for ages 0 to 12, 42% for ages 13 to 18, 37% for ages 19 to 35, 44% for ages 36 to 60, and 15% for ages 61 and over."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
rate_bar(ax, known_age, "AgeGroup", xlabel="Age group (years)")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

:::

*Figure 5. Age distribution of survivors and non-survivors, and survival rate by age group. Use the tabs to switch views. Only passengers with a recorded age are shown.*

The age distributions of survivors and non-survivors overlap heavily, but survivors have a clear extra bump of very young children (Figure 5, Age distribution tab). By group, 61% of children aged 12 or under survived, compared with 37% of passengers aged 19 to 35 and only 15% of those aged 61 or over (Figure 5, Survival by age group tab). Survival rates between ages 19 and 60 ranged from 37% to 44%, so the age effect is most pronounced in the youngest and oldest groups, which are small (46 and 13 passengers). A pattern like this shows up only weakly in a single correlation number.

**Include in the model?** Age is a weak feature overall, so it will not be among our top-correlated features, but the child effect in Figure 5 is real. We keep age in the processed data as an optional feature to test in flexible models. It needs imputation for the 19.7% of passengers with no age.

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 4))
sns.boxplot(data=eda, x="Class", y="FareLog", hue="Outcome", palette=PALETTE,
            order=["First", "Second", "Third"], hue_order=["Did not survive", "Survived"],
```

:::

*Figure 6. Distribution of the log fare for survivors and non-survivors, and the log fare within each passenger class. Use the tabs to switch views.*

Fares are extremely right-skewed (skewness of about 5.0), with a maximum of 512.33 pounds and 9 passengers who paid nothing, so we work with the logarithm of one plus the fare instead of the raw value. Survivors paid more: the median fare was 26.0 pounds for survivors and 9.2 pounds for non-survivors. Part of that is simply passenger class, because fare and class are strongly linked, but within first class survivors generally paid more, while fare distributions overlap considerably within second and third class (Figure 6, Fare within each class tab).

**Include in the model?**  We retain fare in its log form as a candidate feature. It overlaps with passenger class, which we take into account in the feature selection below. However, fare was not among the five predictors selected from the development set.

```{python}
#| fig-alt: "Bar chart: 31% of passengers travelling alone survived versus 51% of those with family."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
```

:::

*Figure 7. Survival rate by family size and by whether the passenger travelled alone. Use the tabs to switch views.*

We combined the number of siblings or spouses and the number of parents or children into a single family size (the passenger plus these relatives). Survival is not a straight-line function of family size. People travelling alone survived approximately 31% of the time, small families of two to four did best (56%, 56%, and 71%), and large families of five or more did worst, with only 21% surviving (Figure 7, Family size tab). Collapsing this into "alone versus with family" keeps the main contrast, 31% versus 51% (Figure 7, Travelling alone tab), in a single clean feature.

**Include in the model?** We retain the travelling-alone indicator and the number of parents and children aboard, which were selected among the five predictors from the development set. The number of siblings and spouses was not selected, while family size remains an optional predictor.

*Figure 8. Survival rate by port of boarding and the mix of passenger classes among passengers boarding at each port. Use the tabs to switch views. One passenger with no recorded port are left out.*

Passengers who boarded at Cherbourg survived more often (approximately 52%) than those from Queenstown (35%) or Southampton (35%). The "Class mix by port" tab offers a likely reason: a substantially higher proportion of Cherbourg passengers travelled first class than those boarding at Southampton. The port effect may therefore partly reflect differences in passenger class.

**Include in the model?**  Although boarding at Cherbourg partly overlaps with passenger class, it was selected among the five predictors from the development set.

```{python}
#| label: plot-cabin-class
#| fig-alt: "Grouped bars of survival by passenger class split by whether a cabin was recorded; a recorded cabin goes with higher survival in every class."
cab = eda.groupby(["Pclass", "HasCabin"])["Survived"].mean().unstack() * 100
cab.index = ["First", "Second", "Third"]
cab.columns = ["No cabin recorded", "Cabin recorded"]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
cab.plot.bar(ax=ax, color=[DIED, SURV], rot=0, width=0.75)
ax.set_ylim(0, 112)
ax.set_xlabel("Passenger class")
ax.set_ylabel("Survival rate (%)")
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
for c in ax.containers:
    ax.bar_label(c, fmt="%.0f%%", padding=2, fontsize=9)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

:::

*Figure 9. Survival rate by title, and by passenger class and whether a cabin was recorded. Use the tabs to switch views.*

Titles pack sex, age and marital status into one feature: "Master" (young boys) survived 60% of the time, while men titled "Mr" survived only 16%, and "Miss" and "Mrs" survived 71% and 79%. This is mostly the sex effect again, with the useful extra detail that boys fared far better than men.

Having a cabin recorded is associated with higher survival rates in every passenger class (Figure 9, Cabin tab). However, these subgroup comparisons should be interpreted cautiously because some groups may contain relatively few passengers. A possible explanation is that cabin numbers were more likely to be recorded for people who survived to be interviewed, but these data cannot test that. Because most cabin information is missing and a recorded cabin is closely tied to first class, we treat it with care.

**Include in the model?** Title overlaps almost completely with sex, so we keep it in the processed data for later experiments but do not select it. The cabin-recorded flag is kept only if it adds something beyond passenger class, which we test in the correlation analysis.

### Columns we exclude

The passenger identifier is only a row number and cannot help predict survival. The name is used only to extract the title. The ticket number is a mix of codes with many unique values; a possible future feature is the number of passengers sharing a ticket, but we leave that out for now to keep the analysis simple.

## Transforming the data for modelling

We now turn the cleaned columns into a form a model can use. The steps are: fill in the missing values using statistics learned **from the training data only**, create the extra features described above, take the logarithm of the fare, and convert categories to 0/1 columns. We deliberately do not scale the numeric columns here. Scaling will be done inside the modelling pipeline, so that its mean and spread are also learned from training data only.

```{python}
#| label: learn-imputation
train_feat = add_simple_features(train)
fill_values = {
    "age_by_title": train_feat.groupby("Title")["Age"].median(),
    "age_overall": train_feat["Age"].median(),
    "embarked_mode": train_feat["Embarked"].mode()[0],
    "fare_by_class": train_feat.groupby("Pclass")["Fare"].median(),
    "fare_overall": train_feat["Fare"].median(),
}
display(fill_values["age_by_title"].rename("Median age (years)").to_frame())
display(fill_values["fare_by_class"].rename("Median fare (pounds)").to_frame())
print("Most common port in the training set:", fill_values["embarked_mode"])
```

*Table 4. Values learned from the training set to fill in missing ages (by title, top), missing fares (by passenger class, middle) and missing ports of boarding (bottom).*

```{python}
#| label: preprocess
TITLES = ["Master", "Miss", "Mr", "Mrs", "Rare"]

def preprocess(df, fv):
    """Impute, engineer and encode features using fill values learned from the training set."""
    out = add_simple_features(df)
    out["Age"] = out["Age"].fillna(out["Title"].map(fv["age_by_title"])).fillna(fv["age_overall"])
    out["Embarked"] = out["Embarked"].fillna(fv["embarked_mode"])
    out["Fare"] = out["Fare"].fillna(out["Pclass"].map(fv["fare_by_class"])).fillna(fv["fare_overall"])
    out["FareLog"] = np.log1p(out["Fare"])
    out["Sex_female"] = (out["Sex"] == "female").astype(int)
    for port in ["C", "Q", "S"]:
        out[f"Embarked_{port}"] = (out["Embarked"] == port).astype(int)
    for t in TITLES:
        out[f"Title_{t}"] = (out["Title"] == t).astype(int)
    return out

FEATURES = [
    "Pclass", "Sex_female", "Age", "SibSp", "Parch", "Fare", "FareLog", "FamilySize",
    "IsAlone", "HasCabin", "AgeMissing", "Embarked_C", "Embarked_Q", "Embarked_S",
] + [f"Title_{t}" for t in TITLES]

train_p = preprocess(train, fill_values)
holdout_p = preprocess(holdout, fill_values)
test_p = preprocess(test, fill_values)

# Every modelling column must now be complete in all three datasets.
for name, d in [("training", train_p), ("held-out", holdout_p), ("test", test_p)]:
    assert d[FEATURES].isna().sum().sum() == 0, f"missing values left in {name} data"
print("No missing values remain in any modelling column.")
train_p[FEATURES].dtypes.value_counts().rename("Number of columns").to_frame()
```

*Table 5. Data types of the modelling columns after the transformations. All 19 columns are numeric.*

All 19 candidate modelling columns are now numeric and complete in the training, held-out test, and original Kaggle test datasets.

## Which features relate most strongly to survival?

We now measure the relationship between every feature and survival, and between the features themselves. We use the Pearson correlation coefficient, which for 0/1 columns is also known as the point-biserial or phi coefficient. It runs from -1 to 1: a positive value means the feature goes up when survival is more likely, and a negative value means the opposite. We compute it on the imputed training set, so the correlation for age includes the filled-in ages.

### Correlation matrix

```{python}
#| label: plot-heatmap
#| column: page
#| fig-alt: "Lower-triangle heatmap of correlations between survival and 18 features. Survival is most positively correlated with being female and with the titles Miss and Mrs, and most negatively with the title Mr and with passenger class. Strong correlations between features include female and the title Mr, boarding at Cherbourg and at Southampton, and passenger class and cabin recorded."
LABELS = {
    "Survived": "Survived", "Pclass": "Passenger class", "Sex_female": "Female", "Age": "Age",
    "SibSp": "Siblings/spouses", "Parch": "Parents/children", "FareLog": "Fare (log)",
    "FamilySize": "Family size", "IsAlone": "Travelling alone", "HasCabin": "Cabin recorded",
    "AgeMissing": "Age missing", "Embarked_C": "Boarded Cherbourg", "Embarked_Q": "Boarded Queenstown",
    "Embarked_S": "Boarded Southampton", "Title_Master": "Title: Master", "Title_Miss": "Title: Miss",
    "Title_Mr": "Title: Mr", "Title_Mrs": "Title: Mrs", "Title_Rare": "Title: Rare",
}
heat_cols = list(LABELS)
corr = train_p[["Survived"] + FEATURES].corr()
heat = corr.loc[heat_cols, heat_cols]
mask = np.triu(np.ones_like(heat, dtype=bool), k=1)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10.5, 8.3))
sns.heatmap(heat, mask=mask, annot=True, fmt=".2f", annot_kws={"size": 7.5},
            cmap="RdBu_r", center=0, vmin=-1, vmax=1, linewidths=0.4, linecolor="white",
            xticklabels=[LABELS[c] for c in heat_cols], yticklabels=[LABELS[c] for c in heat_cols],
            cbar_kws={"label": "Pearson correlation", "shrink": 0.8}, ax=ax)
plt.xticks(rotation=45, ha="right")
plt.yticks(rotation=0)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

*Figure 10. Correlation matrix of survival and the candidate features in the training set. Red means a positive correlation and blue a negative one. Fare is shown on the log scale.*

The first column of the heatmap shows how each feature relates to survival, and the rest shows how the features relate to each other. Three things stand out.

First, the strongest links with survival are being female (0.54), having the title "Mr" (-0.55), travelling in a lower class, meaning a higher class number (-0.37), and the log fare (0.34). Second, several features are close to duplicates of each other. Being female and having the title "Mr" are almost mirror images (-0.88), boarding at Cherbourg and Southampton are nearly opposite (-0.78), a recorded cabin follows passenger class (-0.74), and family size follows the alone flag (-0.71). Third, passenger class and the log fare are also related (-0.70), so they partly carry the same information.

### Ranking the features

Correlation only picks up straight-line relationships, so we also compute the mutual information between each feature and survival, which can detect any kind of dependence. It acts as a second opinion, particularly for age, where the effect is not linear.

```{python}
#| label: rank-features
corr_target = corr["Survived"].drop("Survived")

# Pick the top features by absolute correlation, skipping any that are nearly duplicates
# (|r| >= 0.70) of one we already picked. We rank one representative per idea:
# the title columns (which mostly repeat sex) and raw fare (replaced by log fare) are left out.
CANDIDATES = ["Sex_female", "Pclass", "HasCabin", "FareLog", "IsAlone", "Embarked_C",
              "Age", "Parch", "FamilySize", "SibSp", "AgeMissing"]
K, REDUNDANT_AT = 5, 0.70
selected, rows = [], []
for f in corr_target[CANDIDATES].abs().sort_values(ascending=False).index:
    clash = [(s, corr.loc[f, s]) for s in selected if abs(corr.loc[f, s]) >= REDUNDANT_AT]
    if len(selected) >= K:
        decision, reason = "Not selected", "top five already chosen"
    elif clash:
        decision, reason = "Not selected", f"near-duplicate of {LABELS[clash[0][0]].lower()} (r = {clash[0][1]:.2f})"
    else:
        selected.append(f)
        decision, reason = "Selected", "high correlation, not redundant"
    rows.append([LABELS[f], round(corr_target[f], 3), decision, reason])
selection = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["Feature", "Correlation with survival", "Decision", "Reason"])

mi = pd.Series(
    mutual_info_classif(train_p[FEATURES], train_p["Survived"], random_state=SEED,
                        discrete_features=[f not in ("Age", "Fare", "FareLog") for f in FEATURES]),
    index=FEATURES,
).sort_values(ascending=False)
order = corr_target.abs().sort_values().index
mi_order = mi.sort_values()
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

#### Correlation with survival {.unnumbered}

```{python}

#| fig-alt: "Horizontal bars of the correlation of each feature with survival, led by the title Mr at minus 0.55 and female at 0.54, with the five selected features highlighted."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 6.5))
colors = [SURV if f in selected else "#B0B0B0" for f in order]
ax.barh([LABELS.get(f, "Fare (raw)") for f in order], corr_target[order], color=colors)
ax.axvline(0, color="black", lw=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel("Pearson correlation with survival")
ax.set_ylabel("Feature")
ax.legend(handles=[Patch(color=SURV, label="Selected for modelling"),
                   Patch(color="#B0B0B0", label="Not selected")], loc="lower right")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| fig-alt: "Horizontal bars of the mutual information of each feature with survival, led by the title Mr and female, with age ranking low."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 6.5))
ax.barh([LABELS.get(f, "Fare (raw)") for f in mi_order.index], mi_order.values,
        color=[SURV if f in selected else "#B0B0B0" for f in mi_order.index])
ax.set_xlabel("Mutual information with survival (nats)")
ax.set_ylabel("Feature")
```

:::

*Figure 11. Features ranked by their correlation with survival (sorted by absolute size, with the sign shown by the direction of the bar) and by mutual information with survival. Use the tabs to switch views. Selected features are highlighted.*

```{python}
#| label: selection-table
selection
```

*Table 6. Selection of the five features most strongly correlated with survival, skipping near-duplicates of features already chosen.*

The five features we select are sex, passenger class, travelling alone, boarding at Cherbourg, and the number of parents and children aboard. They come from walking down the correlation ranking and skipping any feature that nearly repeats one already chosen. The "cabin recorded" flag is correlated with survival (0.35) but is skipped because it is strongly associated with passenger class (-0.74), and most cabin values are missing. The title columns are left out of the ranking because they mostly restate sex (-0.88 with the title "Mr"), even though their raw correlations are as high as the top feature. The raw fare is replaced by the log fare, which remains a candidate but was not among the five selected features.

Two caveats matter. The log fare is strongly correlated with passenger class (-0.70), close to our 0.70 cut-off for redundancy, so these two features overlap noticeably. Log fare was not selected among the five development-set predictors. Boarding at Cherbourg has a relatively weak correlation with survival (0.14) and partly reflects passenger class, as seen in Figure 8. The number of parents and children aboard was selected despite its modest correlation with survival (0.11).

The mutual information ranking agrees that sex, title and fare are the most informative. It scores travelling alone (approximately 0.02), parents/children (approximately 0.02) and boarding at Cherbourg (approximately 0.01) much lower, although these features were selected by the correlation-based method. Age scores around 0.05 despite its weak linear correlation with survival (-0.08), consistent with the age-group pattern in Figure 5. Family size is a similar case: its correlation with survival is close to zero (0.04), yet its mutual information (approximately 0.05) is higher than that of travelling alone, which fits the non-linear pattern in Figure 7. We keep age and family size in the processed data as optional features, although they are not among the five selected by correlation.

## Summary of the exploratory analysis

| Feature | Decision | Main reason |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Sex | Include | Strongest single signal (see Figure 4). |
| Passenger class | Include | Survival falls steadily from first to third class and interacts with sex. |
| Fare (log) | Not selected | Survivors paid more, and the log scale reduces extreme skew. However, fare was not among the five features selected from the development set. |
| Travelling alone | Include | People travelling alone survived much less often than those with family. |
| Port: Cherbourg | Include (weak) | Higher survival, but mostly a first-class effect. |
| Age | Optional | Weak by both measures, but children survived more; needs imputation. |
| Title | Optional | Mostly repeats sex; adds boys versus men. |
| Cabin recorded | Drop | Nearly the same as passenger class; mostly missing. |
| Siblings/spouses | Drop | Not among the five selected predictors; travelling alone retains some information about family travel. |
| Parents/children | Include | Selected among the five predictors using the development dataset. |
| Family size | Optional | No linear link, but a non-linear pattern; the alone flag is the simpler version. |
| Passenger ID, name, ticket | Drop | Identifiers, or only useful through the title. |

*Table 7. Summary of our decision for each feature.*

In short, a passenger's chance of survival depended most on being a woman, travelling in a higher class and having paid a higher fare, with smaller contributions from travelling with family and from the port of boarding. About a fifth of the ages and most of the cabins were missing, and the missing values were themselves linked to survival. These findings describe associations in this one historical dataset; they do not show that any single factor caused a passenger to survive.

Two limitations apply to the conclusions above. First, correlation and mutual information look at one feature at a time, so they can miss combinations such as the sex-by-class interaction in Figure 4, and a feature that is weak on its own may still help a model. Second, our development set contains only 623 passengers, so small groups (for example older passengers or the rare titles) give noisy rates, and our selected features should be treated as a starting point that the model comparison can confirm or revise.

## Saving the processed data

We save the processed training and test data to the processed data folder, both using the fill values learned from the training data. The files keep all 19 candidate features, so the modelling stage can choose among them, together with the passenger identifier and, for the training file, the survival outcome. Our five selected features are stored in a short text file so that teammates can load the same list. The held-out test set of 268 passengers is processed using the same imputation values learned from the development set and is kept separate for final model evaluation.

```{python}
#| label: save-processed
KEEP = ["PassengerId"] + FEATURES
train_p[KEEP + ["Survived"]].to_csv(PROC_DIR / "train_processed.csv", index=False)
test_p[KEEP].to_csv(PROC_DIR / "test_processed.csv", index=False)
(PROC_DIR / "selected_features.txt").write_text("\n".join(selected) + "\n")

print("Selected features:", selected)
print(f"train_processed.csv: {len(train_p)} rows x {len(KEEP) + 1} columns")
print(f"test_processed.csv: {len(test_p)} rows x {len(KEEP)} columns")
```

# Predictive modelling with logistic regression

In this section, we build a classification pipeline using logistic regression [@pedregosa2011] combined with feature standardization. Applying standardization inside the modelling pipeline ensures that feature means and standard deviations are learned strictly within each training fold during five-fold stratified cross-validation (using a fixed random seed for reproducibility).

To connect our exploratory findings with the modelling stage without repeating the individual feature analyses, we test whether adding the optional features kept in the processed data (age, family size, and the passenger title indicators for "Master", "Miss", and "Mrs") together with the interaction between sex and passenger class identified in Figure 4 improves cross-validation performance over the five predictors selected independently within each cross-validation training fold.

```{python}
#| label: model-comparison
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold, cross_validate, cross_val_predict
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score, confusion_matrix, roc_curve, accuracy_score, precision_score, recall_score, f1_score

train_mod = pd.read_csv(PROC_DIR / "train_processed.csv")
holdout_mod = holdout_p.copy()
test_mod = pd.read_csv(PROC_DIR / "test_processed.csv")
selected_5 = (PROC_DIR / "selected_features.txt").read_text().strip().splitlines()

for df_m in (train_mod, holdout_mod, test_mod):
    df_m["Sex_x_Pclass"] = df_m["Sex_female"] * df_m["Pclass"]

# Use original ages so imputation is fitted within each CV training fold
train_mod["Age"] = train["Age"].to_numpy()
holdout_mod["Age"] = holdout["Age"].to_numpy()
test_mod["Age"] = test["Age"].to_numpy()

# Restore missing boarding-port values for fold-specific imputation
train_mod["Embarked_C"] = train["Embarked"].map({"C": 1, "Q": 0, "S": 0}).to_numpy()
holdout_mod["Embarked_C"] = holdout["Embarked"].map({"C": 1, "Q": 0, "S": 0}).to_numpy()
test_mod["Embarked_C"] = test["Embarked"].map({"C": 1, "Q": 0, "S": 0}).to_numpy()

extended_cols = selected_5 + [
    "Age", "FamilySize", "Sex_x_Pclass", "Title_Master", "Title_Miss", "Title_Mrs"
]
y_train = train_mod["Survived"]
cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=SEED)
scoring = ["accuracy", "precision", "recall", "f1", "roc_auc"]
def select_fold_features(fold_train):
    # Learn missing-value replacements from this training fold only
    X = fold_train[CANDIDATES]
    X = pd.DataFrame(
        SimpleImputer(strategy="median").fit_transform(X),
        columns=CANDIDATES,
        index=fold_train.index
    )

    # Rank features by correlation with survival
    fold_corr = pd.concat([fold_train[["Survived"]], X], axis=1).corr()
    ranked = fold_corr["Survived"].drop("Survived").abs().sort_values(ascending=False).index

    # Select five features, avoiding near-duplicates
    chosen = []
    for feature in ranked:
        if len(chosen) == K:
            break
        if all(abs(fold_corr.loc[feature, s]) < REDUNDANT_AT for s in chosen):
            chosen.append(feature)

    return chosen

dummy_res = cross_validate(
    DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent"),
    train_mod[selected_5], y_train, cv=cv, scoring=["accuracy", "roc_auc"]
)
cv_rows = [{
    "Model": "Baseline (most frequent outcome)",
    "Number of features": len(selected_5),
    "CV accuracy (mean ± SD)": f"{dummy_res['test_accuracy'].mean():.3f} ± {dummy_res['test_accuracy'].std():.3f}",
    "Precision": 0.0,
    "Recall": 0.0,
    "F1-score": 0.0,
    "ROC-AUC": dummy_res["test_roc_auc"].mean(),
}]

for label, extras in [
    ("Logistic regression (5 selected features)", []),
    ("Logistic regression (5 selected + optional & sex-by-class interaction)",
     ["Age", "FamilySize", "Sex_x_Pclass", "Title_Master", "Title_Miss", "Title_Mrs"]),
]:
    fold_results = []
    fold_counts = []

    for train_idx, val_idx in cv.split(train_mod, y_train):
        fold_train = train_mod.iloc[train_idx]
        fold_val = train_mod.iloc[val_idx]

        # Select features using the training fold only
        fold_selected = select_fold_features(fold_train)
        cols = fold_selected + [f for f in extras if f not in fold_selected]
        fold_counts.append(len(cols))

        pipe = Pipeline([
            ("imputer", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
            ("scaler", StandardScaler()),
            ("logreg", LogisticRegression(C=1.0, max_iter=1000, random_state=SEED)),
        ])

        pipe.fit(fold_train[cols], fold_train["Survived"])

        actual = fold_val["Survived"]
        predicted = pipe.predict(fold_val[cols])
        probabilities = pipe.predict_proba(fold_val[cols])[:, 1]

        fold_results.append({
            "accuracy": accuracy_score(actual, predicted),
            "precision": precision_score(actual, predicted, zero_division=0),
            "recall": recall_score(actual, predicted),
            "f1": f1_score(actual, predicted),
            "roc_auc": roc_auc_score(actual, probabilities),
        })

    results = pd.DataFrame(fold_results)

    cv_rows.append({
        "Model": label,
        "Number of features": round(np.mean(fold_counts), 1),
        "CV accuracy (mean ± SD)": f"{results['accuracy'].mean():.3f} ± {results['accuracy'].std(ddof=0):.3f}",
        "Precision": results["precision"].mean(),
        "Recall": results["recall"].mean(),
        "F1-score": results["f1"].mean(),
        "ROC-AUC": results["roc_auc"].mean(),
    })

display(pd.DataFrame(cv_rows).round(3))
```

*Table 8. Five-fold stratified cross-validation performance comparing the majority-class baseline, logistic regression on five features selected by correlation within each training fold, and logistic regression adding the optional features and the interaction between sex and passenger class.*

Table 8 presents the performance of the logistic regression models evaluated using five-fold stratified cross-validation. The model using five features selected independently within each training fold achieved a mean accuracy of 77.8% (F1 = 0.711; ROC-AUC = 0.829), exceeding the majority-class baseline accuracy of 61.6%. Including the optional predictors and the interaction between sex and passenger class increased mean accuracy to 82.2% (F1 = 0.756; ROC-AUC = 0.870), representing an improvement of 4.4 percentage points over the five-feature model. These findings suggest that the extended model provides better predictive performance on the development data. Performance on the independent held-out test set is reported separately in Section 3.1.

## Diagnostic evaluation and feature weights

We examine out-of-fold predictions and standardized coefficients for the extended logistic regression model using the 623-observation development set. We then evaluate the final model on the independent held-out test set of 268 passengers and generate survival predictions for Kaggle's original 418 unlabeled test observations.

```{python}
#| label: model-diagnostics
ext_pipe = Pipeline([
    ("imputer", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
    ("scaler", StandardScaler()),
    ("logreg", LogisticRegression(C=1.0, max_iter=1000, random_state=SEED)),
])
# Generate out-of-fold predictions with feature selection within each training fold
oof_pred = np.zeros(len(train_mod), dtype=int)
oof_prob = np.zeros(len(train_mod), dtype=float)

for train_idx, val_idx in cv.split(train_mod, y_train):
    fold_train = train_mod.iloc[train_idx]
    fold_val = train_mod.iloc[val_idx]

    fold_selected = select_fold_features(fold_train)
    optional = ["Age", "FamilySize", "Sex_x_Pclass",
                "Title_Master", "Title_Miss", "Title_Mrs"]
    fold_cols = fold_selected + [f for f in optional if f not in fold_selected]

    fold_pipe = Pipeline([
        ("imputer", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
        ("scaler", StandardScaler()),
        ("logreg", LogisticRegression(C=1.0, max_iter=1000, random_state=SEED)),
    ])

    fold_pipe.fit(fold_train[fold_cols], fold_train["Survived"])
    oof_pred[val_idx] = fold_pipe.predict(fold_val[fold_cols])
    oof_prob[val_idx] = fold_pipe.predict_proba(fold_val[fold_cols])[:, 1]
cm = confusion_matrix(y_train, oof_pred)

ext_pipe.fit(train_mod[extended_cols], y_train)
# Evaluate the final model on the held-out test set
y_holdout = holdout_mod["Survived"]
holdout_pred = ext_pipe.predict(holdout_mod[extended_cols])

print("Held-out accuracy:", round(accuracy_score(y_holdout, holdout_pred), 3))
print("Held-out F1 score:", round(f1_score(y_holdout, holdout_pred), 3))
print("Held-out confusion matrix:")
print(confusion_matrix(y_holdout, holdout_pred))
coefs = pd.Series(ext_pipe.named_steps["logreg"].coef_[0], index=extended_cols).sort_values()

test_pred = ext_pipe.predict(test_mod[extended_cols])
test_prob = ext_pipe.predict_proba(test_mod[extended_cols])[:, 1]
pd.DataFrame({
    "PassengerId": test_mod["PassengerId"],
    "Survived": test_pred,
    "PredictedProbability": test_prob.round(4),
}).to_csv(PROC_DIR / "test_predictions.csv", index=False)
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

#### Confusion matrix & ROC {.unnumbered}

```{python}
#| label: plot-cm-roc
#| fig-alt: "Out-of-fold confusion matrix showing 340 true negatives, 44 false positives, 67 false negatives, and 172 true positives, alongside an ROC curve with AUC 0.863."
cm_pct = cm / cm.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True) * 100
annot = np.array([
    [f"{cm[i, j]}\n({cm_pct[i, j]:.1f}%)" for j in range(2)]
    for i in range(2)
])
fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(y_train, oof_prob)
oof_auc = roc_auc_score(y_train, oof_prob)

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.2, 4.1))
sns.heatmap(
    cm, annot=annot, fmt="", cmap="Blues", cbar=False,
    xticklabels=["Pred: Died", "Pred: Survived"],
    yticklabels=["Actual: Died", "Actual: Survived"],
    annot_kws={"size": 10, "weight": "bold"}, linewidths=1, linecolor="white", ax=ax1
)
ax1.set_title("Out-of-fold confusion matrix")

ax2.plot(fpr, tpr, color=SURV, lw=2, label=f"Logistic regression (AUC = {oof_auc:.3f})")
ax2.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], ls="--", color="#888888", lw=1, label="Random baseline (AUC = 0.500)")
ax2.set_xlabel("False positive rate")
ax2.set_ylabel("True positive rate")
ax2.set_title("Out-of-fold ROC curve")
ax2.legend(loc="lower right", frameon=False, fontsize=9)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

#### Standardized coefficients {.unnumbered}

```{python}
#| label: plot-coefs

FEATURE_NAMES = {
    "Sex_female": "Female", "Title_Mrs": "Title: Mrs", "Title_Master": "Title: Master",
    "Title_Miss": "Title: Miss", "FareLog": "Fare (log)", "Embarked_C": "Boarded Cherbourg",

}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 4.2))
colors = [SURV if v > 0 else DIED for v in coefs.values]

ax.set_xlabel("Standardized logistic regression coefficient (log-odds per 1 SD)")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

:::

*Figure 12. Out-of-fold confusion matrix and ROC curve (first tab) and standardized coefficients (second tab) for the extended logistic regression pipeline. Use the tabs to switch views.*

Across the 623 development observations, the extended logistic regression model correctly classified 340 of 384 non-survivors (88.5%) and 172 of 239 survivors (72.0%), with a precision of 79.6% and an ROC-AUC of 0.863 (Figure 12). On the independent held-out test set of 268 passengers, the model achieved an accuracy of 84.3% and an F1 score of 0.784. The held-out confusion matrix showed 150 true negatives, 15 false positives, 27 false negatives, and 76 true positives. Predictions for Kaggle's original 418 unlabeled test observations were generated separately and were not used to calculate performance metrics.

# Discussion and conclusions

Using five-fold stratified cross-validation on the 623-observation development set, logistic regression achieved a mean accuracy of 77.8% (F1 = 0.711; ROC-AUC = 0.829) with five features selected independently within each training fold, compared with 61.6% for the majority-class baseline. Incorporating additional predictors (age, family size, and passenger title indicators) and the interaction between sex and passenger class improved mean accuracy to 82.2% (F1 = 0.756; ROC-AUC = 0.870). On the independent held-out test set of 268 passengers, the extended model achieved 84.3% accuracy and an F1 score of 0.784. These results suggest that the extended logistic regression model provides better predictive performance than the five-feature model. The observed associations involving passenger sex and class are consistent with historical accounts of the evacuation [@hall1986; @elinder2012].

Two main limitations apply to this analysis: (1) our findings describe statistical associations in a single 1912 dataset rather than causal effects, and missing values in age (20%) and cabin (77%) may not be missing completely at random; and (2) we evaluated default ridge regularization with a linear log-odds boundary, where recall on survivors (72.0%) remains lower than specificity on non-survivors (88.5%). An additional limitation is that the held-out evaluation uses a single stratified split, so performance estimates may vary across different partitions of the data. Future work can explore hyperparameter tuning of the regularization strength, probability threshold adjustment, or non-linear classifiers.
